title: Maison Verdier: a classified growth in a canned world? (fictional case)
text: Maison Verdier is a family-owned Bordeaux wine estate founded in 1884. In the 1855-style classification of the region it is ranked as a fifth growth – recognized among the classified estates, but far below the famous first growths. It produces about 300,000 bottles a year of red wine sold at €80–250 per bottle. Like most Bordeaux estates, it sells its wine through négociants (merchants of “La Place de Bordeaux”) who distribute it to importers, restaurants and collectors in 70 countries; wine critics' scores and the classification strongly influence prices.

The environment is changing. Global wine consumption has been declining for years; younger generations drink less alcohol and prefer beer, spirits, cocktails or no-alcohol drinks. The no- and low-alcohol segment grows by about 7 % a year. Climate change brings heat waves, earlier harvests and more variable quality; the appellation rules restrict which grape varieties and practices can be used. US import tariffs on European wine were raised in 2025, and demand from China, once the fastest-growing market, has dropped sharply. Interest rates make holding expensive stocks of aged wine costlier.

Claire Verdier, 38, the founder's great-great-granddaughter, became CEO in 2024 after ten years at a technology company. She wants to “make Verdier relevant for the next generation”. Her plan has three parts: (1) “Verdier Zéro”, a dealcoholized red wine sold in cans at €6 through supermarkets, bars and festivals, under the Verdier name and coat of arms; (2) an app that tells the history of the estate and lets customers buy directly from the château; (3) a US subsidiary that would import and distribute Verdier wines directly to US retailers and restaurants, bypassing négociants.

Reactions are mixed. Some négociants warn that they may reduce allocations for an estate that “sells cans”; a well-known critic wrote that “a classified growth in a can is a contradiction in terms”. Younger consumers in a test market liked the taste of Verdier Zéro, but many did not know what Verdier was. Investors in a sparkling no-alcohol start-up have praised the idea. Several first-growth estates have launched experimental cuvées and art collaborations without any criticism.
